book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: The Core Argument
title: The Core Argument
answer: The core argument is that AI adoption in schools fails or succeeds in predictable ways. It fails when leaders mandate tools they do not use, when districts reward logins and licenses instead of student results, and when governance is skipped. It succeeds when leaders model AI use, when incentives reward hours saved and student outcomes, and when districts publish clear rules about what is allowed, what is required, and who decides.

sections.body: The idea is that the culture and leadership around AI matter more than the tools themselves. The problem it solves is performative adoption, where a district buys licenses, announces initiatives, and reports usage numbers while nothing changes for students. Staff may comply on paper and ignore the tools in practice, which wastes money and breeds cynicism. The text says AI adoption fails when leaders mandate tools without using them, when districts reward usage counts such as logins and licenses instead of results for students, and when governance is skipped. It succeeds when leaders model use, when incentives are tied to hours saved and student outcomes, and when districts publish their rules so everyone knows what is allowed, what is required, and who decides.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the text describes district and school leadership actions rather than grade band specific steps. Leaders show staff how they use AI in their own work and what they have learned. Districts tie incentives to hours saved and student outcomes, not to activity counts, and they publish their rules so everyone knows what is allowed, what is required, and who decides. The text also notes that principals spreading a national AI policy relied on professional learning, shared leadership, and ties with parents and partners. The text does not give separate practices by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as research on school leaders that supports the view. A study of German school leaders found that a digital mindset, marked by agility and empathy, along with leadership that balances exploring new approaches with improving existing ones, predicted how far AI was implemented in their schools (Pietsch & Mah, 2024). A study of Israeli principals spreading a national AI policy found that they relied on professional learning, shared leadership, and ties with parents and partners (Avidov-Ungar & Ganon-Shilon, 2026). The text concludes that leaders who engage deeply get further.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text warns against performative adoption. A district can buy licenses, announce initiatives, and report impressive usage numbers while nothing changes for students. Staff learn to comply on paper and ignore the tools in practice, which wastes money and breeds cynicism that makes real change harder. The text also says adoption fails when governance is skipped and tools spread without rules for privacy, review, and accountability. It does not assign those decisions to a named person, but it says districts should publish their rules so everyone knows what is allowed, what is required, and who decides.
